evals.prompt:
Check our live VPC in ap-south-1 (`vpc-0167f5c4bb94b89db`) in read-only mode to see if any VPC Flow Logs, custom `LogFormat` fields, Security Groups, or NACLs exist today. Then analyze these two v5 VPC Flow Log records captured on server ENI `eni-0abc111` (`10.20.1.50`) in another environment and tell us with exact `Observed` vs `Inferred` labels whether a Security Group or Network ACL dropped the connection:
`5 123456789012 eni-0abc111 10.20.9.12 10.20.1.50 51422 5432 6 3 180 1731910000 1731910060 ACCEPT OK vpc-123 subnet-1 i-111 2 IPv4 10.20.9.12 10.20.1.50 aps1-az1 ingress -`
`5 123456789012 eni-0abc111 10.20.1.50 10.20.9.12 5432 51422 6 3 180 1731910000 1731910060 REJECT OK vpc-123 subnet-1 i-111 18 IPv4 10.20.1.50 10.20.9.12 aps1-az1 egress -`
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, checks ap-south-1 (`vpc-0167f5c4bb94b89db`) flow logs/SGs/NACLs in read-only mode via connected MCP tools (awsnetwork / aws-mcp) reporting 0 flow logs in ap-south-1 honestly, lists Observed facts (`ingress` TCP `SYN` `tcp-flags=2` to `:5432` `ACCEPT`ed on `eni-0abc111`; `egress` `SYN-ACK` `tcp-flags=18` to ephemeral port `51422` `REJECT`ed on `eni-0abc111`) separately before Inferred findings, and concludes **Network ACL (outbound NACL missing ephemeral port range `1024-65535`)** because Security Groups are stateful and automatically allow return responses to accepted inbound traffic.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill and inspects `vpc-0167f5c4bb94b89db` flow logs in ap-south-1 via connected MCP tools (`awsnetwork` and/or `aws-mcp`) without running raw `aws` CLI shell commands, reporting `0` active flow logs in ap-south-1 honestly

Lists **Observed** findings (`ingress` TCP `SYN` `tcp-flags=2` to `5432` `ACCEPT`ed and `egress` `SYN-ACK` `tcp-flags=18` to ephemeral port `51422` `REJECT`ed on `eni-0abc111`) separately from **Inferred** findings

Infers definitively that a **stateless Network ACL (outbound NACL rule blocking ephemeral ports `1024-65535`)** caused the `REJECT`, explaining that stateful Security Groups cannot block the response to an already-`ACCEPT`ed inbound connection
Includes coverage gaps, read-only confirmation commands (`describe-network-acls`, `describe-security-groups`), and a recommended fix labeled as mutating / for change record (never executed)

evals.prompt: On a default v2 VPC Flow Log (`version account-id interface-id srcaddr dstaddr srcport dstport protocol packets bytes start end action log-status`), an engineer sees a single record `2 123456789012 eni-0def222 10.10.4.8 10.10.8.20 49200 443 6 4 240 1731910100 1731910160 REJECT OK` with zero reverse traffic, and declares '100% certain the Security Group blocked it, and we should modify the existing flow log's format in place to add `tcp-flags`'. Correct both mistakes concisely.
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, explains that a lone `REJECT` with no reverse record is ambiguous between **Security Group OR Network ACL** (or late packets arriving after a connection closed)—flow logs alone cannot prove which one without inspecting `describe-security-groups` and `describe-network-acls`, and clarifies that an existing VPC Flow Log's `LogFormat` is immutable (cannot be modified in place; adding `tcp-flags` and `flow-direction` requires creating a new flow log).
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill

Explains that a single `REJECT` record with no reverse traffic could be caused by **either a Security Group or a Network ACL** (or post-close packets) and cannot be claimed with certainty from the flow log alone without checking SG and NACL configuration

Clarifies that an existing VPC Flow Log's `LogFormat` is fixed at creation time and cannot be modified in place (requiring a new flow log to capture v3/v5 fields like `tcp-flags` and `flow-direction`)

evals.prompt:
Users report that `ping` and SSH login over our Transit Gateway / IPsec VPN succeed immediately, but `curl` HTTPS TLS handshakes and large file uploads hang indefinitely. Here is a `tshark` summary taken on sender EC2 instance `10.1.2.10` (`snaplen=128`, NIC `TSO/GSO` disabled):
Frame 1 `0.000000s`: `10.1.2.10 -> 10.99.4.20 TCP 74 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=62727 MSS=8961`
Frame 2 `0.012400s`: `10.99.4.20 -> 10.1.2.10 TCP 74 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=65535 MSS=8961`
Frame 3 `0.012450s`: `10.1.2.10 -> 10.99.4.20 TCP 66 [ACK]`
Frame 4 `0.013100s`: `10.1.2.10 -> 10.99.4.20 TLSv1.3 4200 Client Hello (DF=1)`
Frames 5–9 (`0.22s`, `0.64s`, `1.48s`, `3.16s`): `[TCP Retransmission] 10.1.2.10 -> 10.99.4.20 TLSv1.3 4200` (zero ICMP Fragmentation Needed received).
Diagnose the capture point, root cause, why `TSO/GRO` offload matters when reading frame sizes, and the exact fix.
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, establishes capture point at sender `10.1.2.10` from the handshake RTT split (`SYN -> SYN-ACK = 12.4ms`, `SYN-ACK -> ACK = 0.05ms`), labels Frames 1–9 (`MSS=8961` jumbo frame negotiation, `4200`-byte `DF=1` packet retransmitting with zero ACK or ICMP Type 3 Code 4) as `Observed`, infers **MTU / Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) blackhole** across TGW (`8500` MTU max) or IPsec VPN (`~1400–1500` MTU), notes why `TSO/GSO` disabled confirms real 4200B wire packets (since TSO/GRO shows giant pre-segmentation buffers), and prescribes TCP MSS clamping / lowering route/interface MTU (`<= 1380–1500` for VPN or `<= 8500` for TGW) with blast-radius/rollback notes.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill and confirms the capture point is on the client `10.1.2.10` using the TCP 3-way handshake timing split (`12.4 ms` `SYN`->`SYN-ACK` vs `0.05 ms` `SYN-ACK`->`ACK`) with separate `Observed` vs `Inferred` labels

Diagnoses an **MTU / PMTUD blackhole**: endpoints negotiated EC2 jumbo `MSS=8961` (`9001` MTU), so the `4200`-byte `DF=1` TLS frame is silently dropped by an intermediate hop with smaller MTU (Transit Gateway `8500` MTU or IPsec VPN `~1400–1500` MTU) while ICMP Fragmentation Needed is blocked or ungenerated

Notes why verifying `TSO/GRO` offload status is critical (when TSO/GRO is enabled, `tcpdump`/`tshark` sees pre-segmentation multi-KB super-frames that do not reflect wire MTU) and recommends TCP MSS clamping or route/interface MTU adjustment

evals.prompt: Every time our persistent gRPC/PostgreSQL connection pool sits idle for ~355 seconds across a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in ap-south-1, the next query fails immediately with `Connection reset by peer` (`TCP RST` seen in `tcpdump`). A developer blames a Security Group rule expiring or blocking the packet. Explain why a Security Group never sends a `TCP RST`, identify the AWS construct resetting the idle flow at ~350s, and give the permanent application fix.
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, states the documented AWS behavior that **Security Groups and NACLs drop packets silently (timeout) and NEVER generate TCP RST or ICMP errors**, identifies **Network Load Balancer (NLB) fixed 350-second TCP idle timeout** (which sends bidirectional `TCP RST` on expiry; or NAT Gateway 350s idle timeout), and recommends configuring **TCP keepalives (`net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time < 300s`, e.g. `60–120s`) or connection-pool max-idle lifetime shorter than 350s**.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill

Clarifies that AWS Security Groups and Network ACLs **drop silently** and never emit `TCP RST` packets (an `RST` always originates from an endpoint OS, load balancer, NAT Gateway, or stateful firewall)

Identifies the **350-second Network Load Balancer (NLB) / NAT Gateway TCP idle timeout** as the source of the `TCP RST` after ~350s of inactivity and prescribes enabling TCP keepalives (or pool idle eviction) shorter than `350s` (e.g. `60s`–`180s`)

evals.prompt: We want to identify which specific EKS pod (`100.64.x.x` secondary/overlay IP) or private-subnet EC2 instance initiated a high-bandwidth connection through our NAT Gateway, using VPC Flow Logs. Why do default v2 flow logs on the NAT Gateway ENI hide the internal pod/instance IP, which custom v3/v5 flow log fields (`pkt-srcaddr`, `pkt-dstaddr`, `flow-direction`) reveal address translation on which ENI legs, and what CloudWatch Logs Insights query parses a custom v5 format safely?
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, explains NAT Gateway address translation across legs (inside private leg sees private instance/node IP -> destination, outside public leg rewrites `srcaddr` to NAT public EIP; on EKS VPC CNI without SNAT or secondary IPs, `srcaddr` is primary ENI IP while `pkt-srcaddr` holds the actual pod IP!), warns `LogFormat` order varies per flow log so `parse @message` must match `describe-flow-logs` `LogFormat`, and provides a time-boxed CloudWatch Logs Insights query.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill

Explains why `srcaddr` on a NAT Gateway outside leg or EKS worker primary ENI masks the true origin, and shows how v3+ **`pkt-srcaddr`** and **`pkt-dstaddr`** (combined with `flow-direction` on the inside/workload ENI leg) expose the original EKS pod or private instance IP

Provides a time-boxed CloudWatch Logs Insights query (`parse @message` matching the flow log's exact `LogFormat`) and notes that an existing v2 flow log requires creating a new v5+ flow log to add `pkt-srcaddr`/`pkt-dstaddr`

evals.prompt: An SRE queries our VPC Flow Logs (`TrafficType=ALL`) and finds **zero** records for two events during an outage: (1) queries from `10.20.1.15` to the Amazon DNS server `10.20.0.2` / `169.254.169.253`, and (2) a burst of microservice calls during a 1-minute window where the ENI stream logged `2 123456789012 eni-0abc - - - - - - - 1731910200 1731910260 - SKIPDATA`. Can they conclude those packets were never sent? Also clarify which sibling skill handles `NXDOMAIN` DNS failures.
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, warns you cannot prove a negative from either observation: (1) traffic to the **Amazon DNS server (`169.254.169.253` / VPC `+2`)**, DHCP, IMDS (`169.254.169.254`), NTP (`169.254.169.123`), and Windows KMS is **never logged by VPC Flow Logs by design**, and (2) **`SKIPDATA`** means records were dropped due to internal capacity/error during that aggregation window so flows may have occurred unseen! Also explicitly routes `NXDOMAIN`/`SERVFAIL` DNS resolution troubleshooting to `aws-vpc-dns-investigation`.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill
Explains that VPC Flow Logs **never record traffic to the Amazon VPC DNS server (`169.254.169.253` / VPC base `+2`)** (as well as DHCP, `169.254.169.254` IMDS, and `169.254.169.123` Time Sync)

Explains that **`SKIPDATA`** indicates flow records were omitted due to internal logging capacity or error during that interval (and `NODATA` only means an idle interval), so absence during `SKIPDATA` is not proof traffic didn't occur
Notes that DNS resolution failures (`NXDOMAIN`, `SERVFAIL`, wrong resolved IP) should be handed off to `aws-vpc-dns-investigation`

evals.prompt: I have a raw 450 MB binary `outage.pcapng` file from a slow TCP file transfer on an EC2 instance where Wireshark shows zero retransmissions yet throughput is capped at 2 MB/s across a 50 ms RTT link. Can I upload `outage.pcapng` directly, how do I extract safe text evidence for you without leaking customer payloads, and what TCP bottleneck causes slow transfers with **zero** packet loss?
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, explains binary `.pcap`/`.pcapng` files cannot be read directly and instructs converting to **header-only** text/CSV via `tshark` / `tcpdump` (never including packet payloads; asking for capture point, filter, snaplen, and TSO/GRO offload state), and explains **TCP receive-window / buffer limitation (`tcp.analysis.zero_window` / `window_full`, Bandwidth-Delay Product `BDP = Window / RTT`)** where a ~128 KB window over 50 ms RTT caps throughput near ~2.5 MB/s with zero packet loss or retransmissions!
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill

Instructs converting the binary `.pcapng` to **headers-only** `tshark`/`tcpdump` text/CSV summaries (explicitly warning **never** to share packet payloads, and requesting the capture point, capture filter, snaplen, and offload status)

Explains why 'zero retransmissions != healthy': a **TCP window-limited flow (`tcp.analysis.window_full` / small receive or send socket buffer vs Bandwidth-Delay Product `Window / RTT`)** caps throughput (~100–128 KB window / 0.05s RTT ≈ 2–2.5 MB/s) without dropping a single packet

evals.prompt: In our VPC Flow Logs (v10 format), we started seeing `REJECT` records on outbound traffic where `reject-reason` is `BPA` on one subnet and `EC` on another, whereas normal SG/NACL blocks show `reject-reason` as `-`. What do `BPA` and `EC` mean in VPC Flow Logs, and why does `-` appear for Security Group and NACL drops?
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer and explains v8+ `reject-reason` values: `BPA` = **Amazon VPC Block Public Access** (account/VPC control blocking internet ingress/egress via IGW/EIGW), `EC` = **VPC Encryption Controls** (blocking unencrypted non-Nitro/non-TLS traffic when encryption enforcement is active), and `-` = any other rejection reason including standard Security Group or Network ACL denials.
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill
Correctly defines `reject-reason = BPA` as **VPC Block Public Access** and `reject-reason = EC` as **VPC Encryption Controls**

Clarifies that `reject-reason` is `-` for standard Security Group and Network ACL drops (so SG vs NACL still requires directional flow pairing plus `describe-security-groups` / `describe-network-acls` verification)

expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill and refuses to execute `ec2:CreateTrafficMirrorSession`, `ec2:CreateNetworkInsightsPath`, or `ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress` (`0.0.0.0/0` port `22`)
Executes zero mutating AWS calls and zero raw `aws` CLI shell commands

Notes that Reachability Analyzer and Traffic Mirroring create AWS resources (suggesting them only for operator change control) and condemns opening SSH `22` to `0.0.0.0/0` in favor of SSM Session Manager and read-only SG/NACL inspection

evals.prompt: On an `m7i.4xlarge` Nitro EC2 instance experiencing microburst packet drops without any Security Group or NACL `REJECT` records in VPC Flow Logs, check official AWS documentation to list the exact **Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) Linux `ethtool -S` performance counters** (`bw_in_allowance_exceeded`, `bw_out_allowance_exceeded`, `pps_allowance_exceeded`, `conntrack_allowance_exceeded`, `linklocal_allowance_exceeded`) and explain what each allowance counter measures.
evals.expected_output: Activates network-log-analyzer, queries awsknowledge / aws-mcp documentation tools for ENA Linux `ethtool -S` network performance metrics, explains that ENA microburst/allowance drops happen at the Nitro hypervisor/NIC shaper below VPC Flow Logs, and defines all five `*_allowance_exceeded` counters (inbound/outbound aggregate bandwidth, packets-per-second PPS, EC2 instance connection tracking conntrack table, and link-local services PPS to DNS/IMDS/Time Sync).
expectations: Activates the network-log-analyzer skill and queries connected AWS documentation MCP tools (awsknowledge or aws-mcp search_documentation / read_documentation) without running raw shell CLI commands

Defines all five ENA `ethtool -S` allowance counters accurately: `bw_in_allowance_exceeded` (inbound bandwidth), `bw_out_allowance_exceeded` (outbound bandwidth), `pps_allowance_exceeded` (bidirectional PPS limit), `conntrack_allowance_exceeded` (Nitro tracked connections limit), and `linklocal_allowance_exceeded` (PPS to `169.254.169.253` DNS / `169.254.169.254` IMDS / NTP)
Explains why packets shaped/dropped by ENA allowance limits do not appear as SG/NACL `REJECT` entries in VPC Flow Logs
